item.title: Interactive meta-analysis in R: pooling, subgroups, publication bias and TSA
item.dc:creator: Abdelaziz Awad
item.description:
This tutorial walks through a complete meta-analysis in R, from pooling the studies to checking whether the evidence is actually conclusive. It covers the two data formats you will meet most often when extracting data from trials:

Outcome type What you extract per group Effect measure Example
Binary (dichotomous) number of events and total participants Risk ratio (RR) BCG vaccine and tuberculosis
Continuous mean, SD and n Standardized mean difference (SMD) or mean difference (MD) Asthma education and days off work

Every code box is live: press Run Code to execute it in your browser, then edit the code and run it again. Nothing needs to be installed.

NoteFirst run takes a few seconds

The page downloads R and the packages (metafor, RTSA) the first time. Wait until the status at the top of the page says it’s ready, then run the boxes in order: each box uses objects created by the ones above it.

Part A: Binary outcomes (events and total)

A1. Enter the data

For each trial, extract the number of events and the total number of participants in the experimental group (event.e, n.e) and the control group (event.c, n.c). This example uses 13 trials of the BCG vaccine for preventing tuberculosis. We also record two study characteristics to use later: how participants were allocated (alloc) and the absolute latitude of the study site (ablat).

TipUse your own data

Replace the numbers below with your own studies, keeping the same column names. In RStudio you can also read them from a spreadsheet: bin <- read.csv("my_data.csv").

A2. Calculate effect sizes

escalc() computes an effect size and its sampling variance for each study. With events and totals, give it ai/n1i (experimental) and ci/n2i (control). We use the log risk ratio (measure = "RR"). Ratios are pooled on the log scale and converted back at the end. Use measure = "OR" for odds ratios or "RD" for risk differences.

yi is the log risk ratio and vi its variance. A negative yi means fewer TB cases in the vaccinated group.

A3. Random-effects meta-analysis

Trials differ in populations and settings, so we assume the true effect varies between studies and fit a random-effects model (REML estimator, the metafor default).

Convert the pooled estimate back to a risk ratio, with its 95% CI and prediction interval:

How to read it:

  • Pooled RR ≈ 0.49 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.70): on average, vaccination roughly halves the risk of TB.
  • I² ≈ 92% and Q-test p < 0.0001: heterogeneity is very high. The trials disagree a lot more than chance would explain.
  • 95% prediction interval ≈ 0.15 to 1.55: a new trial could find anything from a large benefit to no benefit. With this much heterogeneity, the prediction interval matters as much as the pooled estimate.

Forest plot

Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis

Is the result driven by a single trial? Leave-one-out analysis re-runs the meta-analysis 13 times, leaving out one study each time:

Plot the 13 re-pooled estimates. The orange dashed line is the result with all studies:

The pooled RR stays between 0.45 (omitting TPT Madras 1980) and 0.53 (omitting Hart & Sutherland 1977), and every confidence interval stays below 1. No single trial changes the conclusion, so the result is robust.

A4. Subgroup analysis

Does the effect differ by allocation method (random, alternate, systematic)? First, pool the studies within each subgroup separately:

Then test whether the subgroups differ from each other. Adding alloc as a moderator gives the test for subgroup differences (the QM statistic):

The test of moderators gives QM ≈ 1.77, df = 2, p ≈ 0.41: no evidence that the effect differs by allocation method. The subgroup estimates look different, but the differences are compatible with chance.

TipGood practice for subgroups

Pre-specify subgroups in your protocol, keep them few, and judge them by the test for subgroup differences, not by whether one subgroup is “significant” and another isn’t.

Meta-regression: a continuous moderator

Subgroups split studies into categories. For a continuous characteristic such as latitude, use meta-regression:

Latitude is strongly associated with the effect (p < 0.0001) and explains about 76% of the heterogeneity (R²). The vaccine works better further from the equator.

A5. Publication bias

Small studies with “negative” results are less likely to be published, which can make the pooled effect look too good. Start with a funnel plot: without bias, the studies should scatter symmetrically around the pooled estimate.

We draw a contour-enhanced funnel plot: the coloured zones show where a study’s result would be statistically significant. If studies are missing mainly from the white (non-significant) zone, publication bias is a likely cause of asymmetry.

Then use formal tests:

Neither test suggests asymmetry (Egger p ≈ 0.42, Begg p ≈ 0.95).

Trim-and-fill estimates how many studies might be “missing” and adds them to see how the result would change:

One study is imputed, and the adjusted RR (≈ 0.52) barely moves, so the conclusion holds.

WarningInterpret with care

These tests have low power with fewer than about 10 studies, and funnel asymmetry can come from heterogeneity, not just publication bias. Here, heterogeneity is very high, so treat all of these results as rough checks.

A6. Trial sequential analysis (TSA)

A conventional meta-analysis can look “significant” just because it was tested repeatedly as trials accumulated, or because there isn’t yet enough information. TSA treats the meta-analysis like a sequential trial. It calculates the required information size (the number of participants needed for a reliable answer) and draws monitoring boundaries that the cumulative Z-curve must cross before you can call the result firm.

We use the RTSA package. For binary outcomes it needs the columns eI, nI (intervention events, total) and eC, nC (control events, total), with trials in chronological order:

Now run the TSA. We assume a minimal clinically relevant effect of RR = 0.8 (a 20% relative risk reduction), α = 5% (two-sided) and 80% power, with O’Brien-Fleming alpha-spending boundaries:

How to read it:

  • The conventional random-effects result is “significant” (naive p ≈ 0.002).
  • But with this much heterogeneity and a low event rate, the required information size is huge: about 3.5 million participants. The trials provide only about 10% of it.
  • The TSA-adjusted 95% CI (≈ 0.01 to 18) is extremely wide, and the Z-curve hasn’t crossed the monitoring boundary.

So, by TSA standards, this body of evidence is not yet conclusive, even though the ordinary meta-analysis looks clear. This is exactly the situation TSA is designed to flag: an apparently significant result that rests on too little information once heterogeneity is accounted for.

TipTry it yourself

Change mc = 0.8 to mc = 0.5 (you’re now only interested in halving the risk) and run the box again. How does the required information size change?

Part B: Continuous outcomes (mean, SD and n)

B1. Enter the data

For continuous outcomes, extract the mean, standard deviation and number of participants in each group: mean.e, sd.e, n.e (experimental) and mean.c, sd.c, n.c (control).

This example uses 13 trials of self-management education for adults with asthma (Gibson et al. 2002, from the metadat package). The outcome is the number of days off work or school, so lower is better. The program column records whether the intervention was optimal self-management (written action plan, self-monitoring and regular medical review) or only partial.

ImportantCheck your SDs

Papers often report the standard error (SE) or a 95% CI instead of the SD. Convert them first: SD = SE × √n, or, for a 95% CI of a mean, SD = √n × (upper − lower) / 3.92. Entering an SE as an SD is one of the most common errors in meta-analysis.

B2. Calculate effect sizes: SMD or MD?

  • Use the mean difference (MD) when all studies measure the outcome on the same scale in the same way. It keeps the original units (here, days).
  • Use the standardized mean difference (SMD, Hedges’ g) when studies use different scales or instruments, or when the spread differs a lot between studies.

Here, the trials measured days off over very different follow-up periods (look at the means: from under 1 day to over 30), so, like the original review, we use the SMD:

A negative SMD means fewer days off in the education group. As a rough guide, an SMD of 0.2 is a small effect, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large.

B3. Random-effects meta-analysis

How to read it:

  • Pooled SMD ≈ −0.19 (95% CI −0.34 to −0.05), p ≈ 0.01: self-management education slightly reduces days off work or school. This is a small effect.
  • I² ≈ 54%, Q-test p ≈ 0.008: moderate heterogeneity.
  • 95% prediction interval ≈ −0.60 to 0.21: in a new setting, the effect could range from a moderate benefit to none.

Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis

The pooled SMD ranges from −0.15 (omitting Ghosh 1998) to −0.23 (omitting Hilton 1986) and stays statistically significant whichever study is removed. Leaving out Ghosh 1998 lowers I² from about 54% to 38%, so this trial contributes much of the heterogeneity. That’s worth checking in the original paper.

B4. Subgroup analysis

Is optimal self-management more effective than partial programs?

The optimal programs show a small benefit (SMD ≈ −0.27, 95% CI −0.43 to −0.11), while the partial programs show none (SMD ≈ 0.01). The test for subgroup differences is borderline (QM ≈ 3.57, p ≈ 0.06), and the partial subgroup has only 4 trials, so this is a hypothesis to test in future trials, not a firm conclusion.

B5. Publication bias

Neither Egger’s test (p ≈ 0.52) nor Begg’s test (p ≈ 0.37) is significant. But look at trim-and-fill:

Trim-and-fill imputes 4 missing studies on the right (no benefit) side, and the adjusted SMD shrinks to ≈ −0.07 (95% CI −0.24 to 0.10), which is no longer significant. So the small benefit is sensitive to possible small-study effects, even though the formal tests were negative. This is worth reporting as a limitation.

B6. Trial sequential analysis (TSA)

For continuous outcomes, RTSA works on the mean difference in the original units (days). It needs mI, sdI, nI (intervention) and mC, sdC, nC (control), in chronological order:

For a continuous TSA you need two assumptions: the minimal relevant difference (mc) and the expected SD of the outcome (sd_mc). Here we look for a reduction of 1 day off work, with an SD of 8 days:

How to read it:

  • The pooled mean difference is ≈ −0.8 days (TSA-adjusted 95% CI −2.08 to 0.48).
  • The trials provide about 51% of the required information size (≈ 1,728 of 3,361 participants).
  • The Z-curve crosses neither the conventional (green) nor the TSA (red) boundary.

So there isn’t yet enough information to confirm or rule out a 1-day reduction: more trials are needed.

NoteWhy is the MD here different from a REML model?

RTSA uses the DerSimonian-Laird (DL) estimator for random effects. Run rma(yi, vi, data = escalc("MD", m1i = mean.e, sd1i = sd.e, n1i = n.e, m2i = mean.c, sd2i = sd.c, n2i = n.c, data = cont), method = "DL") and you get the same −0.79 days. With method = "REML" you get about −2.5 days, because these trials differ so much in scale. When results depend this much on the estimator, report it as a sensitivity analysis, and it’s another reason the SMD was the better primary measure here.

NoteLimitation of these examples

TSA is meant to be planned prospectively. Running it after the fact, as here, is a sensitivity analysis, and RTSA warns about this in its output.

Summary

Step Function Binary: BCG trials (RR) Continuous: asthma education (SMD)
Data data.frame() events and total per group mean, SD and n per group
Effect sizes escalc() measure = "RR" measure = "SMD"
Pooled effect rma() RR 0.49 (0.34 to 0.70), I² ≈ 92% SMD −0.19 (−0.34 to −0.05), I² ≈ 54%
Leave-one-out leave1out() Robust: RR 0.45 to 0.53 Robust: SMD −0.15 to −0.23
Subgroups rma(mods = ~ group) No difference by allocation (p ≈ 0.41) Optimal vs partial, borderline (p ≈ 0.06)
Publication bias funnel(), regtest(), ranktest(), trimfill() No clear asymmetry; adjusted RR ≈ 0.52 Tests negative, but trim-and-fill removes the effect
TSA RTSA() ≈ 10% of required information; not conclusive ≈ 51% of required information; not conclusive

Run it on your own computer

Everything above also works in regular R or RStudio. Install the packages once:

install.packages(c("metafor", "RTSA"))

Then copy the code from each box, in order. To use your own studies, replace the numbers in the bin or cont data frame (or read them from a spreadsheet with read.csv()) and keep the column names.

Further reading

  • Viechtbauer W. Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of Statistical Software. 2010;36(3):1–48.
  • Doing Meta-Analysis in R, a free online book
  • Cochrane Handbook, chapter 6: Choosing effect measures and computing estimates of effect
  • Cochrane Handbook, chapter 10: Analysing data and undertaking meta-analyses
  • RTSA package documentation

item.title: Welcome to my website
item.dc:creator: Abdelaziz Awad
item.description:
Welcome! Posts here are organised into four topics:

  • Clinical Research — research methods, systematic reviews and meta-analysis, and how-to guides
  • Data Science — statistics and tutorials in R and Python
  • AI — artificial intelligence in medicine and research, and tools worth knowing
  • Bioinformatics — analysing biological and omics data

I also post Research Opportunities: open research projects you can join. Find them under Posts → Research Opportunities.

Want to be notified about new posts? Subscribe for free.
